title: A Ni(OH)2 symmetric battery cell for hydroxide exchange membrane-based direct air capture of CO2 - Nature Energy
gist: A University of Delaware/RepAir DAC team demonstrates a symmetric Ni(OH)2 battery-based hydroxide exchange membrane cell (HEMCC) for direct air capture of CO2, reporting 132 kJ per mol CO2 energy cost and 5,000-hour lab durability plus a 48-hour pilot-scale (9x300 cm2) run, with a projected cost pathway below $100 per tonne CO2 via technology learning rates; the enabling PiperION membrane and the RepAir DAC scale-up partner are both commercially tied to the paper's senior author.

insights.claim: A symmetric Ni(OH)2 battery cell with a hydroxide exchange membrane (HEMCC) captured CO2 from ambient air at an energy cost of 132 kJ per mol CO2 (0.83 MWh per tonne CO2) in a scaled-up 9x300 cm2 pilot electrochemical stack tested continuously over 48 hours.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: This energy-cost figure is a direct benchmark against thermal-swing DAC (e.g. Climeworks/Carbon Engineering-style solid sorbent or liquid solvent systems) and other electrochemical DAC concepts; investors tracking carbon-removal economics should compare against it directly.
insights.quote: a scaled-up 9 × 300 cm2 electrochemical stack achieved an energy cost of 132 kJ molCO2−1 and flux of 0.19 molCO2 m−2 h−1 equivalent to 0.83 MWh tCO2−1 and 75 kgCO2 m2 yr−1

insights.claim: The pilot-scale stack achieved a CO2 flux of 0.19 mol CO2 per m2 per hour (75 kg CO2 per m2 per year) while meeting the 300 Pa pressure-drop requirement needed for practical DAC air-contactor engineering, a design constraint the authors say prior electrochemical DAC papers have largely ignored.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Pressure drop and flux together determine fan/blower energy and land/footprint requirements for a real DAC facility -- most prior lab-scale electrochemical DAC demos skip this, so meeting it here is a credibility signal for scale-up feasibility.
insights.quote: the pilot-scale stack meets the 300 Pa pressure drop requirements for DAC

insights.claim: A laboratory-scale 25 cm2 version of the same Ni(OH)2/hydroxide-exchange-membrane cell ran durably for 5,000 hours (over half a year) of continuous testing, addressing the electrode-degradation problem that has limited prior electrochemical carbon-capture concepts.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Durability, not just headline energy cost, has been the main technical barrier for electrochemical DAC; a >5,000-hour result is the key proof point for whether this chemistry can survive an industrial duty cycle.
insights.quote: a symmetric nickel hydroxide battery design with a hydroxide exchange membrane durably tested in a laboratory-sized 25-cm2 device for 5,000 h

insights.claim: The authors project a pathway to below US$100 per tonne of CO2 captured for this Ni(OH)2-based electrochemical DAC approach by applying energy-technology learning-rate curves -- the same cost-decline logic historically observed for batteries, solar panels and LED lighting -- across successive technology generations.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A sub-$100/tonne DAC cost target, if realized, would make electrochemical DAC cost-competitive with the US DOE's Carbon Negative Shot goal and would materially change the addressable market for voluntary/compliance carbon removal credits.
insights.quote: A pathway to below US$100 tCO2−1 is presented on the basis of energy technology learning rates, showcasing electrochemical DAC as a potential climate change solution.

insights.claim: Because the HEMCC process runs on renewable electricity and avoids the thermal-swing regeneration step (heating a sorbent to release captured CO2) used by conventional DAC, it bypasses the dominant cost driver that has kept thermal DAC systems expensive.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Electrification of the capture step (rather than heat) ties DAC cost to falling renewable electricity prices instead of fuel/heat costs, a structurally different cost curve than incumbent thermal DAC players.
insights.quote: Electrochemical carbon capture is a promising low-energy-cost solution for direct air capture (DAC) by using renewable electricity and avoiding traditional, energy intensive thermal swing sorption.

insights.claim: The cell captures CO2 by cycling nickel between its Ni(OH)2 and NiOOH states: charging converts Ni(OH)2 to NiOOH and raises local pH to capture CO2 as carbonate, while discharge reverses the reaction and releases purified CO2 -- the same redox couple used in nickel-metal-hydride batteries, repurposed for gas separation rather than energy storage.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Reusing mature, low-cost battery-grade nickel hydroxide chemistry (rather than exotic electrocatalysts) for DAC is a cost and supply-chain advantage versus platinum-group-metal or novel-material based electrochemical capture approaches.

insights.claim: Cyclic voltammetry showed the Ni(OH)2-to-NiOOH oxidation peak at 1.44 V vs RHE, with the parasitic oxygen-evolution reaction (OER) onset at only 1.52 V vs RHE and the reverse NiOOH-to-Ni(OH)2 reduction peak at 1.28 V vs RHE -- a narrow 0.08 V window between useful oxidation and wasteful OER that the team must manage to control efficiency.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The tight margin before parasitic oxygen evolution kicks in is the key efficiency-loss mechanism engineers will need to widen (via catalyst or electrolyte tuning) to push energy cost further below the reported 132 kJ/mol.

insights.claim: Electrochemical precipitation of Ni(OH)2 onto nickel foam is done by sacrificing the counter electrode's own metal -- it lost 0.57 g of nickel (27% of its initial mass) during a 4-hour deposition while the working electrode gained 0.83 g of active material -- an in-situ, self-consuming electrode fabrication method rather than an externally sourced coating process.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A self-sacrificing in-situ deposition process could simplify manufacturing and lower electrode production cost versus externally sourced active-material coatings, relevant to scale-up capex assumptions.
insights.locator: Extended Data Fig. 2: Electrochemical precipitation of Ni(OH)2 onto nickel foam

insights.claim: Electron efficiency during cell operation peaked at 0.32 but averaged only 0.25 across a full cycle, a meaningful gap between best-case and typical performance that represents clear headroom for further engineering improvement.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The 0.25-to-0.32 efficiency gap quantifies how much energy-cost improvement is plausible from operating-point optimization alone, before any new materials are needed -- a near-term, low-risk lever for cost reduction.

themes.theme: Commercialization structure and conflicts of interest

insights.claim: The hydroxide exchange membrane used in the cell, PiperION, is supplied by Versogen, a company for which senior/corresponding author Yushan Yan is founder and CEO and co-author Brian P. Setzler is a co-founder -- meaning the paper's core enabling material is produced by the corresponding author's own commercial venture.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The membrane supply chain for this technology runs through a company the lead academic founded and leads, a material conflict-of-interest to weigh when assessing claims of the membrane's performance and availability.
insights.quote: Y.Y. is the founder and CEO, and B.P.S. is a co-founder, of Versogen, the producer of PiperION.

insights.claim: Scale-up of the technology is being pursued by RepAir DAC Ltd (Zichron Ya'akov, Israel), co-founded by Yushan Yan and Ben Achrai, and four of the nine listed authors (Naama Y. Gluz, Maurice Artoul, Jean-Philippe Hiegel and Ben Achrai) are RepAir DAC employees who led the durable-electrode, stack-hardware, MEA optimization and techno-economic analysis work.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: This academic paper functions as a technical validation of an existing DAC startup's (RepAir DAC) pilot stack design, not just a neutral university study -- relevant context for any investor diligencing RepAir DAC or comparable electrochemical DAC startups.
insights.quote: Y.Y. and B.A. are co-founders of RepAir DAC Ltd, the scale-up company. B.A, N.Y.G, M.A. and J.-P.H. are employed by RepAir DAC Ltd.

insights.claim: The research was funded by the US Department of Energy's National Energy Technology Laboratory (award DE-FE0031955) and the US Department of Defense Army Research Laboratory (award W911NF-23-2-0028), showing continued federal (DOE and DOD) interest in funding electrochemical carbon-removal R&D.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Federal DOE/DOD funding for this specific chemistry signals government-backed derisking of electrochemical DAC ahead of any DOE Carbon Negative Shot or related procurement programs.
